item.content:encoded:
Novo's Wegovy pill helps patients lose about 6% of weight in three months, real-world data show Reuters | Updated: 14-11-2026 22:45 IST | Created: 14-11-2026 22:45 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

By Patrick Wingrove LONDON Nov 14 - Patients who stayed on Novo Nordisk's daily Wegovy pill lost an average of 6.2% of their body weight over three months, according to real-world data due to be presented at the ObesityWeek conference in Washington. The pill, launched in January, has helped Novo regain some ground lost to Eli Lilly, and the Danish drugmaker is trying to stay ahead of its US rival in the race for oral obesity treatments. Novo's Chief Scientific Officer Martin Holst Lange said in an interview that the real-world data was encouraging as it broadly replicated the findings of 5.5% weight loss at 12 weeks seen in Novo's late-stage trial for the pill. Study participants, who started taking the pill between January 5 and February 7, 2026, lost an average of 6.3 kg (13.9 pounds) from a baseline weight of 103.0 kg (227 pounds), Novo said. About three-fifths lost at least 5% of their weight, and roughly one in six lost at least 10%. The analysis covered 5,872 adults on the Ro telehealth platform who had never taken a weight-loss drug and who stayed on the pill for the full three months. Novo Nordisk's fortunes have declined significantly since it became Europe's most valuable listed company following the 2021 launch of its injectable weight-loss drug, Wegovy. Its stock has plummeted over 70% from its peak as Lilly surpassed it to take the lead in the obesity-drug market. According to company presentations earlier this month, however, oral treatments now represent roughly a third of US obesity prescriptions, with Novo securing over 80% of new oral prescriptions. The company in September said separate real-world data showed patients who switched from weight-loss injections to Novo's pill continued to lose weight. Oral Wegovy — known chemically as semaglutide — led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, while Eli Lilly's obesity pill Foundayo led to about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, separate studies have shown.

item.content:encoded:
SpaceX launches 15th Starship flight with hopes of achieving first round trip Reuters | Updated: 14-11-2026 05:36 IST | Created: 14-11-2026 05:36 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

SpaceX launched the 15th flight of its Starship spacecraft from Texas on Friday on a mission the company hopes will be the first round-trip rocket voyage to orbit and back to the very spot where it left Earth, a key test of Elon Musk's effort to build a fully reusable rocket system. Plans call for Starship's uncrewed upper-stage vessel to re-enter the atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit and return to its launch tower on Saturday for an engine-controlled touchdown assisted by the giant mechanical arms of a pioneering catch-landing mechanism. SpaceX had intended to use the same return-flight and "chopstick"-arm technology to recover Starship's lower-stage booster rocket shortly after the two parts of the spacecraft separated within minutes of the launch. But the Super Heavy booster, for reasons not immediately clear, was diverted from its return flight path to a fixed point over the Gulf of Mexico and momentarily hovered in the air before exploding a short distance over the sea surface. SpaceX mission controllers hoped to have better luck in steering Starship's upper stage back to home base at the end of its flight. The vehicle reached orbit about 27 minutes after launch, SpaceX said. KEY TEST OF REUSABILITY Bringing the top portion of the spacecraft intact back to the platform where it was launched would mark a breakthrough in the ambitions of Musk, who founded SpaceX in 2002, to reduce spaceflight costs by developing a fully recyclable rocket system. The combined vehicle, consisting of the main Starship cargo-and-crew vessel perched atop its Super Heavy booster rocket and standing 40 stories high, roared off its launch pad from SpaceX's South Texas Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville. The flight marked Starship's 15th test flight since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites to orbit. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavor for SpaceX's satellite-connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a rocket ship still under development. Starship 15 began releasing its cargo of 26 satellites about 36 minutes into its flight in a payload-delivery operation expected to take less than an hour to complete, the company said in a livestream presentation of the mission. Musk's space and AI business views Starship as key to expanding its network of Starlink internet satellites and, in the future, deploying a swarm of orbital AI data-processing centers dubbed Starmind, as the company positions itself to become a high-tech infrastructure provider. SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and a payload of satellites to orbit for the first time despite some rocket engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an upper stage splashing down intact into the Pacific Ocean before bursting into flames. RETURN-FLIGHT AND RECOVERY PLANS For Friday's mission, the company was aiming for both the lower-stage Super Heavy and the upper-stage Starship to return to the spacecraft's Texas launch site for safe landing and recovery. Plans called for the orbital cruise vessel to touch down about 22 hours after launch. SpaceX has said it would be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" if that feat is achieved. SpaceX has previously returned the 236-foot (72-meter) Super Heavy booster three times to its launch pad after sending Starship to space, with the booster flying itself back to Earth minutes after launch and gently descending upright into the grasp of a pair of large mechanical arms fixed to the launch tower. The last such "tower catch" was in March 2025. It was not immediately clear why Friday's attempt failed. Starship was expected to descend from space after completing 14 orbits around Earth, setting up its debut catch landing for Saturday afternoon. Musk has said he expects to achieve a pace of weekly Starship launches by the first half of 2027. NASA has helped fund Starship's development with roughly $3.2 billion since selecting the rocket ship in 2021 to serve as a lunar lander for its astronauts under the multibillion-dollar Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion of its own funds into the rocket's development. NASA and SpaceX expect Starship to land humans on the moon by 2028, though several major testing objectives remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back. Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship tanker rockets in orbit, a critical process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA's Orion capsule, in Earth's orbit next year for Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA's planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV.

item.description: An internet trade group sued New York on Friday, seeking to block a state law requiring social media platforms that contain potentially addictive features to provide state-approved warning labels ...
item.content:encoded:
New York sued over law requiring social media 'warning label' Reuters | Updated: 14-11-2026 05:34 IST | Created: 14-11-2026 05:34 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

An internet trade group sued New York on Friday, seeking to block a state law requiring social media platforms that contain potentially addictive features to provide state-approved warning labels for users. In a complaint filed in federal court, NetChoice said the law violates the free speech protections of the US Constitution's First Amendment by compelling its members to convey the state's "preferred message" about online safety. The office of New York Attorney General Letitia James, who enforces the state's laws, declined immediate comment. NetChoice has more than 30 members including Alphabet's Google and YouTube, Facebook and Instagram parent Meta Platforms, Snapchat parent Snap and ByteDance's TikTok. It has filed many lawsuits challenging regulation of social media businesses. Signed by Governor Kathy Hochul last December, the New York law requires social media platforms with infinite scrolling, auto-play and algorithmic feeds to warn about potential harm to younger users. It requires the display of a "warning" from the US Surgeon General that while social media may benefit some young users, "excessive use may be associated with significant mental health harms." The statement is modeled after findings in 2023 by former US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy. NetChoice said New York's law is "designed to block, burden, and browbeat social media users" by subjecting them to the warning when they sign on and after multiple hours of use, with no way to bypass it. "Unlike a static warning on a product label, these warnings repeatedly interrupt users and block access to protected speech," NetChoice said. NetChoice filed a similar lawsuit against California last month. It also said New York's law is similar to a Colorado law that a federal judge blocked in November 2025, citing the First Amendment. Colorado is appealing that decision. New York's law is scheduled to take effect on January 1.

item.description: Polish President Karol Nawrocki vetoed legislation on Friday that would have let regulators decide whether online content is illegal and order it blocked, his second rejection of a bill ...
item.content:encoded:
Polish President Nawrocki vetoes digital content bill for second time Reuters | Updated: 13-11-2026 22:48 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 22:48 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Polish President Karol Nawrocki vetoed legislation on Friday that would have let regulators decide whether online content is illegal and order it blocked, his second rejection of a bill implementing the European Union’s Digital Services Act. Nawrocki said the bill, which had been narrowed and resubmitted after he vetoed an earlier version in January, gave state officials excessive power over online speech. "It is not the role of an official to rule on whether a given piece of content constitutes a crime or not. That is solely the role of independent courts," he said in a video on X. The bill, which the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, passed in October, would have let regulators order the blocking of online content including criminal threats and incitement to violence, with appeals routed through courts. Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist opposition, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-European coalition government have clashed repeatedly since he took office, as the president has vetoed 48 of the government's bills. The legislation had gained urgency after a string of knife attacks at Polish schools in October, including one in which a 15-year-old wore a helmet-mounted camera and appeared to intend to film the attack. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the veto would leave Poland without the tools the government says are needed to respond quickly to such cases. "This veto is not just throwing legislation in the trash — it’s permission for hate, hatred and the death that the internet also brings," Gawkowski said in a post on X. Nawrocki rejected the link between the bill and the school attacks, accusing the government of exploiting the violence to push the legislation through. "They exploited a tragedy, applied emotional blackmail, to push through regulations that give the government essentially arbitrary control and the ability to decide what we can and cannot say, write or publish," he said. Tusk defended the bill in a post on X. "Protecting children from online criminals. It is hard to imagine a more important issue that should unite people across political divides. And yet he vetoed it," Tusk said. Gawkowski told a press conference he would draft another bill on the issue.
